title: Aristotle's Poetics: Final Project
author: Jacob Allee
summary: Jacob Allee, writing for Study the Great Books, turns Aristotle's Poetics into a practical framework for judging modern stories, and in particular movies, which he calls the descendants of the Greek stage. He walks through Aristotle's six parts of a play in their order of importance: Plot, Character, Thought, Diction, Song and Spectacle. Plot receives the longest treatment, with beginning, middle and end, magnitude, unity, universality, the evoking of fear or pity, and the split between simple and complex plots using reversal, recognition and scenes of suffering. Character is broken into moral purpose, propriety, being true to life and consistency, while the later elements are tied to modern equivalents such as dialogue, film scores and CGI. He argues that spectacle should support the story and never replace it. The piece closes with a concrete assignment in which students critique a chosen film against each category, using a note-taking worksheet.
points: Aristotle ranks the parts of a story as Plot, Character, Thought, Diction, Song and Spectacle, and the author shows this order still explains why some films satisfy and others do not.
A good plot has a true beginning, middle and end, a magnitude the audience can take in at once, and unity that cuts anything not advancing the single action.
Characters must be moral agents whose choices reveal them, who act with propriety, who are believable, and who are consistent, even when consistently inconsistent.
Modern spectacle such as CGI is acceptable only when it supports the story, and the author warns that visual dazzle can crowd out real storytelling.
The closing assignment gives teachers a ready classical exercise that applies primary-source theory to a familiar modern medium through a structured viewing worksheet.
quotes: Plot is properly of first importance in regard to the components of a story for the obvious reason that Plot is to Character as Water is to Fish. The Plot forms the world wherein the characters of the story can live and move and have their being.
A story with no structure, no intentional arrangement of the incidents meant to bring about a certain conclusion, is aimless and conveys little meaning.
Functionally he suggests cutting anything extraneous, that which does not support or advance the plot toward the end or which really properly belongs to another story other than the one being told.

Concerning character, a good man does not suddenly do a heinously wicked thing, nor does an unbelievably wicked man show genuine charity and good will toward his neighbor without a series of incidents which explain such a change.
Thought is the manifestation of a character’s reasoning which undergirds their actions in the story.

Diction is important because even if a story has a cohesive plot and believable characters who express their thoughts in a way that is perfectly consistent with their nature and circumstances, still those thoughts should be written in a powerful and persuasive way.
Ideally, however, Spectacle is meant to support, not supplant, the story the writer has made. A good play or movie does not subvert the role of story-telling for the sake of mere spectacular effects.
In light of Aristotle’s notions of what makes for a good story, and particularly a stage production, evaluate a modern movie and critique it according to his standards.
